extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (line bundles and curves)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and numerical tests for properties of invertible sheaves/linear series on projective curves (base-point-freeness, separation of points/tangents, very ampleness), plus classification facts for low-genus curves (genus 0,2,3, hyperelliptic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for L to be base-point-free
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and for every closed point p one has h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p)) = 1, then L is base-point-free and hence induces a morphism from C to projective space (Theorem 15.2.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the equality shows there exists a section of L not vanishing at p, so p is not a base point. This criterion is applied pointwise: verify the drop in h0 after twisting down by a single point is exactly 1 for all closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a linear series to separate points
rubrics_metrics.description: If p and q are distinct closed points of degree 1 and h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p−q)) = 2, then the linear series L separates the points p and q (the induced map f satisfies f(p) ≠ f(q)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (by repeated application of Remark 19.2.6), the equality h0(C, L) = h0(C, L(−p)) + 1 = h0(C, L(−q)) + 1 = h0(C, L(−p−q)) + 2 shows there is a section vanishing at q but not at p, giving a hyperplane through f(q) not through f(p). Use this test for every pair of points to check separation of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for separating tangent vectors at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a closed point of degree 1 and h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−2p)) = 2 (equivalently h0(C, L(−p)) − h0(C, L(−2p)) = 1), then the map corresponding to L separates tangent vectors at p (the cotangent map is surjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: there exists a section of L vanishing at p to order exactly 1 (not to order 2). This produces a function on the target vanishing at f(p) whose pullback has a simple zero at p; hence the cotangent map is nonzero/surjective onto a 1-dimensional space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for L to be very ample (closed embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for all closed points p and q (not necessarily distinct) one has h0(C, L) − h0(C, L(−p−q)) = 2, then L gives a closed embedding into projective space (it separates points and tangent vectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the point-separation and tangent-separation tests: verifying the stated equality for every ordered pair (p,q) establishes that the associated morphism is injective on points and injective on tangent spaces, hence a closed embedding by Theorem 19.1.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical degree criteria for base-point-freeness and very ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and deg L ≥ 2g then L is base-point-free. If deg L ≥ 2g + 1 then for any basis of sections the induced morphism [s0, ..., s_{deg L − g}] is a closed embedding (so L is very ample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a blunt numerical criterion usable without checking h0 drops at every point: verify degree bounds relative to genus g. Remember: deg L ≥ 2g ⇒ base-point-free; deg L ≥ 2g+1 ⇒ very ample (embedding into P^{deg L − g}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness criterion on curves (numerical)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a projective, regular, integral curve over k, an invertible sheaf L is ample if and only if deg L > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the specialization of the Nakai–Moishezon criterion to curves: ampleness reduces to positivity of degree. The text notes this can be extended to non-algebraically-closed fields and gives pointers to exercises that remove the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion/classification: genus 0 curve with a rational point
rubrics_metrics.description: If C has genus 0 and admits a k-valued (degree 1) point p, then C ≅ P^1_k (Proposition 19.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea used: take L = O(p) of degree 1, then h0(C, L) = 2 and the two sections give a closed embedding into P^1; the only closed embedding of C into P^1 forces C ≅ P^1. Thus existence of a k-point is the only obstruction (over non-algebraically-closed fields) to being P^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of genus 0 curves as plane conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any genus 0 curve can be described as a conic in P^2: the degree-2 line bundle L = ω_C^∨ has deg L = 2 and gives a closed embedding into P^2; the image is scheme-theoretically contained in a conic (kernel of Sym^2 H0(C,L) → H0(C,L^{⊗2}) nontrivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Riemann–Roch to compute dimensions of spaces of sections; the map Sym^2 H0(C,L) → H0(C,L^{⊗2}) has domain dimension 6 and codomain 5, forcing a nontrivial quadratic relation cutting out a conic containing the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/criterion for hyperelliptic curve
rubrics_metrics.description: A (projective regular integral) genus g curve C is hyperelliptic if it admits a degree-2 morphism (double cover) π: C → P^1_k. Equivalently (Exercise 19.5.B), for g ≥ 1 C admits a degree-2 invertible sheaf L with h0(C, L) = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we say C is hyperelliptic we usually have in mind a chosen double cover π; for g ≥ 2 the hyperelliptic map (if it exists) is unique (Proposition 19.5.7). To check hyperellipticity one may check for a degree-2 line bundle with exactly two independent global sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperelliptic Riemann–Hurwitz branch count
rubrics_metrics.description: For a double cover π: C → P^1 by a projective regular irreducible genus g curve (char k ≠ 2, k algebraically closed), π has 2g + 2 branch points (Theorem 19.5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the specialized Riemann–Hurwitz formula for degree-2 covers: use explicit affine models y^2 = f(x) with f squarefree of degree r to relate r to genus g (r = 2g + 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification/uniqueness of double covers by branch points (char ≠ 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not 2: given r distinct points p1,...,pr on P^1, there is precisely one double cover branched at exactly those points if r is even (Proposition 19.5.2). The cover can be written locally as y^2 = f(x) with f monic squarefree whose roots are the branch points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses two affine patches y^2 = f(x) on Spec k[x] and z^2 = u^r f(1/u) on Spec k[u] glued via z = y/x^{r/2} when r is even; when r is odd an exercise analyzes the obstruction. Over non-algebraically-closed k there are twist issues classified by k^×/(k^×)^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 2 curves are hyperelliptic (canonical criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g = 2 then ω_C has degree 2 and h0(ω_C) = 2, so ω_C is base-point-free and induces a degree-2 map C → P^1; hence every genus 2 curve is hyperelliptic and corresponds to a double cover of P^1 branched over 6 points (19.6.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a natural bijection between genus 2 curves and degree-2 covers of P^1 up to automorphisms of P^1; use Riemann–Roch and earlier base-point-free criteria to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical embedding test for genus ≥ 3 (nonhyperelliptic case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For g > 1, if C is not hyperelliptic then the dualizing sheaf ω_C gives a closed embedding into P^{g−1} (Exercise 19.7.A). In genus 3, ω_C is base-point-free and gives a map to P^2; this map is a closed embedding iff C is not hyperelliptic, in which case C is represented as a quartic plane curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check base-point-freeness via h0 computations (Riemann–Roch). To test embedding in genus 3, examine whether there exist p,q with h0(ω_C) − h0(ω_C(−p−q)) = 1: if so, the canonical map fails to be injective and C is hyperelliptic; otherwise the canonical map is an embedding producing a degree-4 plane curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical model in genus 4: complete intersection criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonhyperelliptic genus 4 curve C, the canonical map embeds C as a sextic curve in P^3; such canonical curves are (and conversely) complete intersections of a quadric surface and a cubic surface in P^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: compute h0(C, i^* O_{P^3}(2)) via Riemann–Roch and compare with h0(P^3, O(2)) = 10 to deduce existence of at least one quadric containing C; further analysis shows C lies scheme-theoretically as intersection of a quadric and a cubic. Use ranks of quadrics to exclude planar containment.
